**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verse 2:**

﴿And a Book inscribed﴾, written in an orderly fashion, for the *sattr* is the arrangement of written letters. What is meant by it, according to al-Farra', is the book in which deeds are recorded, which the servant is given on the Day of Resurrection in his right hand or his left. This is the book mentioned in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find laid open﴾ [al-Isra' 17:13]. Al-Kalbi said it is the Tawrah (Torah). It was also said that it is the Injil (Gospel), and the Zabur (Psalms). It was said that it is the Qur'an, and it was said that it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). In al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit), it says: it is not appropriate that any of these opinions be taken as definite; rather they are presented as possibilities. As for the indefiniteness (*tankir*, the grammatical state of a noun lacking the definite article), it was said: it is for generic singularity (*al-ifrad nw'an*), and that is according to the view that there are multiple such books. Or it is for singularity of individual (*al-ifrad shakhsan*), and that is according to the opposing view. Its benefit is to indicate that it is distinguished within the category of books by a matter that sets it apart from the rest. The preferable reading, in both cases of indefiniteness, if it is taken to refer to one of the two books, namely the Qur'an and the Tawrah, is that it falls under the pattern of ﴿that He may reward a people﴾ [al-Jathiyah 45:14]. Thus in the indefiniteness there is the perfection of definition, and an alert that this Book is not obscure, whether it is indefinite (*nakkara*) or definite (*'urrifa*).

Of this kind is the indefiniteness (tankir) in His words, ﴿in an unrolled parchment﴾. The word raqq is pronounced with a fatha or a kasra, and Abu al-Sammal recited it with a kasra. It means a thin skin on which something is written, and its plural is ruqq. According to Majma' al-Bayan, its root is from al-lam'an (the glimmer), as in the saying: "taraqraqa al-shay'" (the thing shimmered) when it gleamed. Or it may be from al-ruqqa (thinness), the opposite of al-safaqa (thickness), as has been said. It has been used figuratively for whatever scribes write on, such as tablets and other things.

Al-manshur means spread out. It has been said that describing it this way indicates the soundness of the book and its freedom from error, since it is placed open to the view of every observer, secure from objection because it is free of anything that would call for it. It has also been said that the description explains its state, which the verse mentioned just before this one contains, on the basis that what is meant is the records of deeds. It may also show that it is made manifest to the angels, peace be upon them, who refer to it easily in their affairs, on the basis that it is the Preserved Tablet. Or it is for people, so that nothing prevents them from reading it and being guided by its guidance, on the basis of the other opinions.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), "manshur" is read as "mansukh" (copied out), spanning what lies between the east and the west.

If this is considered together with what preceded from him a moment ago, explaining it as "the restrained," it will also be one of the words with contrary meanings. Munabbih ibn Sa'id said: it is Jahannam, called a sea because of its vastness and its fullness. The fitting connection between the clauses, once what the speech is directed toward is determined, is clear. It is here the affirmation of the emphasis of the punishment of the Hereafter and the confirmation of its existence and occurrence. Exalted is He swore by matters all of which indicate the perfection of His power, may He be glorified and exalted, while they are also connected with the origin and the return. Moreover, it is known that the Torah is written by the Jews today only on parchment, and it seems they took this from their predecessors. The Imam said: It is possible that the wisdom in the oath by "the Tur," "the inhabited House," and "the sea that is set ablaze" is that they are places of solitude for three prophets with their Lord, exalted is He. As for the inhabited House, it is for the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and he said there: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah. Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87]. So, for its honor through that, Allah, exalted is He, swore by it. As for the mention of the Book, it is because the prophets had speech in these places, and speech is in the Book. As for the mention of the raised canopy, it is to show the elevation of the inhabited House, so that the greatness of the status of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, may be known. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verses 9–10:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿On the Day when the sky will sway violently﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarfiyyah). Its governing verb (nāṣib) is either "wāqi'" (will occur), or "dāfi'" (will repel), or the sense of negation, with the implication that the repelling of it will not be negated except on that day. This is according to considering the principle of implication (mafhūm), and there is no harm in it, since it does not contradict reality, because He, the Exalted, gave them respite in this world and did not neglect them. Makki (Makki ibn Abi Talib) prohibited that it be governed by "wāqi'," but no proof for the prohibition was mentioned, and there appears to be no proof for it either. The meaning of "tamur" (sways violently) is "taḍṭarib" (is agitated), as Ibn 'Abbas said, i.e., it shakes while remaining in its place. In another report from him, it is "tushaqqaq" (is split). Mujahid said: "tadur" (revolves). The root of mawr (violent motion) is repeated coming and going; it was said to be moving with a wave-like agitation, and it was said to be rapid flowing, and it is said of running in general. They cited the verse of al-A'sha:

"As if her gait, from the house of her neighbour, were the mawr of a cloud, neither slow nor hasty."

﴿And the mountains will move, moving﴾ from the surface of the earth, so that they become scattered dust (habā'an munbatha). The use of the two verbal nouns (maṣdarān) signals their strangeness and their departure from the familiar limits, i.e., a wondrous swaying and a marvellous movement whose true nature cannot be grasped.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verse 15:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ This is a rebuke and a reproach to them, since they used to call it magic, as if it were said: "You used to say of the revelation with which I warn you that it is magic. ﴿Or do you not see?﴾ That is: "Or are you blind to what is being reported, just as you were blind to the news in the world?" The particle fa' (then) indicates what has been mentioned. This is because, since it requires a preceding conjunct to which the sentence "its magic" can be correctly subordinated, and since this sentence is an address of reproach like "this is the Fire..." etc., it was necessary to supply that conjunct in a way that makes the subordination correct and is indicated by the context: ﴿So recount﴾, i.e., "you used to say," and so on. This is also indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in vain talk, playing﴾ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny.﴾ In al-Kashshaf, it is stated that this is like when you argue with a proof and the opponent says, "This is false," so you bring a proof clearer than the first, silencing him, and you say: "Is this false?!" You reproach him by holding him to account for the fact that his earlier statement was false. In such a case it is permissible to suppose the word "say" with the meaning "Would you say this is false?", and it is also permissible not to suppose it, because it is built upon the words of the opponent; and this is more eloquent. ("Or") as is evident, is disjunctive (munqati'ah). In al-Bahr, when they were told "This is the Fire," they paused at the two possibilities through which doubt could enter as to whether it is the Fire: either it is ("then") magic that deceives the very sight, or there is a defect in the observer's vision. The apparent reading is that he made ("or") equivalent (mu'addalah), and the first is further from the point.

**﴿Enter it and endure it, or do not endure it; it is all the same for you.﴾** That is, enter it and experience its hardships; then do whatever you wish of patience or its absence.

**﴿It is all the same for you.﴾** That is, the two matters are equal for you in terms of their being of no benefit, since neither one repels the punishment or lightens it. Here "sawa'un" (سواءٌ) is the predicate of an omitted subject, and it is valid to predicate it of the dual because it is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar). It has also been permitted that it be the subject with an omitted predicate, but this is not the best view. The words of the Exalted, **﴿You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.﴾**, serve as the reason for the equality, for since the recompense is certain to occur, owing to the prior announcement of the threat and to God's decree according to His justice, patience and its absence are equal in not being of benefit.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verse 17:

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and bliss.﴾ This begins the mention of the state of the believers after the mention of the state of the disbelievers, as is the custom of the Glorious Qur'an in warning (tarhib) and giving glad tidings (targhib). It is also permissible that it be part of what is said to the disbelievers at that time, as an increase in their grief and distress; but the first (view) is more apparent. The tanwin (nunation) in both places is for magnification, meaning: in great gardens and a great bliss. It is also permissible that it be for specification of kind (nau'iyyah), meaning: a kind of gardens and a kind of bliss specific to them. That it is a substitute (ʿiwad) for the genitive noun, meaning "their gardens and their bliss," is not strong, as is not hidden.

﴿Fakihin﴾ (enjoying, taking delight) [meaning] delighting in ﴿what their Lord has given them﴾ of bounty. It is also read ﴿fakihin﴾ without an alif. In both readings it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the concealed pronoun in the prepositional phrase ﴿in gardens﴾, which is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾ (indeed). Khalid read ﴿fakihun﴾ with a nominative ending, as the predicate itself, with ﴿in gardens﴾ depending on it, but it was placed before it for emphasis. Whoever permits the predicate to be multiple also permits it to be a predicate following another predicate. ﴿And their Lord protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾ is coordinated with ﴿in gardens﴾ on the assumption that the latter is a predicate, as if it were said: they dwell [in gardens and their Lord protected them], etc. Or it is coordinated with ﴿given﴾ if ﴿ma﴾ is taken as a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), meaning: enjoying their Lord's giving and their protection from the punishment of the Blazing Fire. Many did not permit its coordination with it if ﴿ma﴾ is taken as a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), since the meaning would then be: enjoying what their Lord protected them with, which would leave no returning pronoun to the relative. Some permitted it by supposing a returning pronoun, meaning: He protected them with it, the preposition ﴿bi﴾ being for accompaniment. In al-Kashf [it is said]: it was not interpreted as omitting the returning pronoun, because of the frequency of such omission, even though it is attested in prose. The verb is one that takes three objects, and this is heard from some [Arabs]. It is not hidden that this is also a sound view, and the meaning is more firmly established on it, because enjoyment (fukāha) is a pleasure that its possessor is occupied with, and the pleasure of the giving may admit of renewal according to the multiplicity of what is given, whether in protection [or otherwise]. On the verbal-noun reading, [this] is not the case. I say: perhaps this is what comes to mind first. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial qualifier, with or without ﴿qad﴾, either of the concealed pronoun in the predicate or in the circumstantial qualifier, or of the subject of ﴿atā﴾ (gave), or of its object, or of both. The mention of ﴿Rabb﴾ (Lord) in the place of the pronoun, as an annexed noun to their pronoun, is for honour and as a reason. Abu Ḥaywa read ﴿waqqāhum﴾ with the qāf doubled.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verse 19:

﴿Eat and drink with wholesome enjoyment﴾. That is: it is said to them, "Eat and drink" (kulu washrabu) with wholesome eating and drinking (aklan wa-shurban hanian), or "with food and drink that is wholesome" (taaman wa-sharaban hanian). Thus the speech is with an implied verb of saying (taqdir al-qawl). And "hanian" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (mafʿul mutlaq, al-masdariyya), because it is an adjective of a verbal noun. Or it is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul bihi). In either case, the two verbs (al-fi'lan) compete for it (tanazaʿahu, the grammatical phenomenon called tanazuʿ, "competition" of verbs for a single complement). Al-hanii (the wholesome) is everything in which no hardship is involved and whose aftermath is not unpleasant (wakhamuhu, its consequence).

﴿for what you used to do﴾. That is: by means of it (bisababihi) or in exchange for it (bimuqabalatihi). The "ba'" (bi-) in both cases is connected (mutaʿallliq) to "kulu washrabu" by the principle of tanazuʿ. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the "ba'" be extra (za'ida), and what follows it be the subject (fa'il) of "hanian", as in the verse of Kuthayyir:

Wholesome, pleasant, free from any lingering sickness, for the honor of our reputations, which he (the one who violated them) has made lawful.

For "ma" in it is the subject of "hanian", since it is in origin an adjective in the sense of a verbal noun whose verb is necessarily omitted due to frequent usage, as if it were said: "It was wholesome for the honor of the one who made lawful our reputations." In that case, just as it is permitted to make "ma" here the subject with the extra "ba'" in the sense of "hanna'akum ma kuntum taʿmalun" (may it bring you joy in what you used to do), it is also permitted to make the subject a pronoun referring back to the eating or drinking indicated by its verb. However, there is an objection: the addition of a particle to the subject has not been established by transmission (sama') as common usage in a non-subject position like "kafa," according to some disagreement, nor is it analogical (qiyasiyya) in a case like this. Moreover, the speech still requires an implied noun (taqdir mudaf), namely "the recompense of what you used to do," etc., and this involves a kind of artificiality (takalluf).

**﴿Reclining﴾** is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl, a term for a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). Abu al-Baqa said: it is a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿eat﴾ or in ﴿He has protected them﴾ or in ﴿He has given them﴾ or in ﴿enjoying﴾, or from the adverbial phrase, meaning "in gardens." Abu Hayyan preferred the last of these options. **﴿On couches﴾** is the plural of sarīr (couch), a known object, and it is also pluralized as asirrah. It is derived from surūr (joy), since it belongs to people of blessing. The naming of a dead person's bier as a sarīr is an optimistic omen (tafā'ul) of the joy that reaches the deceased upon returning to the neighborhood of God, the Exalted, and being freed from the prison of this world. Abu al-Sammal read surar with a fatḥah on the rā'. This is a dialect feature of the tribe of Kalb in doubled (geminated) roots, to avoid a sequence of two ḍammahs with gemination.

Page 32

**﴿Arranged in rows﴾** means placed in a row and a straight line. **﴿And We will marry them to wide-eyed houris﴾** means We will join them with them. This is what al-Raghib said. Then he said: the Qur'an does not use "We married them to houris" in the way one says "I married him to a woman," which signals that this is not according to the customary form of marriage among us. Al-Farra' said: "tazawwajtu bi-imra'ah" is the dialect of Azd Shanu'ah. The well-known view is that the verb tazawwaja takes one object directly, while zawwaja takes two objects. It has been said that the bā' here is there to imply a meaning in the verb of joining (qarān) or attachment (ilṣāq). This was objected to on the grounds that it implies the meaning of marriage by contract, which does not fit the context, since a contract does not take place in Paradise, as it is not a place of obligation, or else the bā' indicates causation, and marriage here does not mean giving someone in marriage, but rather making them into pairs, that is, We made them so by means of wide-eyed houris. Ikrimah read bi-ḥūri ʿīnin with the genitive construction of the qualified noun with its adjective, following the well-known interpretation.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who believed﴾, and so on, is a resumptive statement (*istiʾnāf*, a new sentence that begins afresh), given to explain the condition of a group of the people of Paradise, after the condition of all of them has been explained. They are those whose offspring shared their faith. The relative pronoun (*al-mawṣūl*) is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and its predicate is ﴿We shall join them﴾. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and their offspring followed them﴾, is a conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) upon ﴿those who believed﴾. It has also been said that it is a parenthetical clause (*iʿtirāḍ*) giving the reason. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿with faith﴾, is connected to the following (*al-ittibāʿ*), meaning: their offspring followed them with a faith that, in general terms, falls short of the rank of the faith of the fathers. This is either in itself, based on the varying degrees of faith itself, or in regard to the absence of deeds like the deeds of the fathers being joined to it. Mentioning this restriction serves to indicate that the ruling applies to complete faith in its own right, not by way of joining. It has been said that ﴿with faith﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) of "the offspring," and it has been said that it is a circumstantial clause of the pronoun (in "them"), with its nunation (*tanwīn*) signifying glorification. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause of both, with its nunation signifying indefiniteness.

The reliable interpretation is what we have already mentioned: ﴿We shall join them with their offspring﴾ in rank.

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Hannād, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim and al-Bayhaqī in his *Sunan* reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Indeed God, Exalted is He, raises the offspring of a believer to be with him in his rank in Paradise, even if they are below him in deeds, so that his eye may be comforted by them." Then he recited the verse. Al-Bazzār and Ibn Mardawayh also reported it from him, traced back (*marfūʿan*) to the Prophet (ﷺ).

In the narration of Ibn Mardawayh and al-Ṭabarānī, also from him, he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said: When a man enters Paradise, he asks about his parents, his wife and his children. It is said to him: They have not attained your rank and your deeds. He says: O Lord, I worked for myself and for them. So it is commanded that they be joined to him." Ibn ʿAbbās then recited the verse.

The apparent meaning of the report is that the intended meaning of joining them to the fathers is their residing with them, not merely their being raised up to them and occasionally connected to them, even for a visit. That this applies generally is not far from the bounty of God, Mighty and Majestic. As for what has been said, namely that it may be specific to some and not to others, this is a restriction of His vast kindness, exalted is His majesty. Some have found support for such specification in what is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Those who believed are the Emigrants and the Helpers, and the offspring are the Successors (*tābiʿūn*)." But I do not think this is authentic.

﴿And We shall not deprive them﴾, that is, We shall not diminish the fathers by this joining, ﴿of their deeds﴾, that is, of the reward of their deeds, ﴿of anything﴾, that is, of any amount, by giving some of their rewards to their children, so that their rewards would be reduced and their rank lowered. Rather, We raised them to their position purely by favour and kindness.

Ibn Zayd said: The pronoun refers to the children, meaning: "We did not deprive the joined children of the recompense of their good and bad deeds at all; rather, We did this for them after their recompense for their deeds, in full." But this is not correct, even though Abū Ḥayyān said that this possibility is made good by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned﴾. The first interpretation was adopted by Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr and the majority. The verse, according to the view of the majority, refers to adult offspring. Mundhir ibn Saʿīd said: it refers to young children.

It is reported from al-Ḥabr (Ibn ʿAbbās) and al-Ḍaḥḥāk that they said: "God, Exalted is He, joins the young children, even if they did not reach the age of faith, with their believing fathers." [Page 33] Those who hold this view take the phrase "with faith" as connected to "We joined," meaning: We joined by means of the faith of the fathers, their young children who died before reaching the age of obligation, so they are in Paradise with their fathers. It has been said that whoever holds this view explains "their offspring followed them" as "they died and followed in their footsteps before reaching puberty." It is also permitted that "with faith" be connected to "followed," in the sense that they followed them with this attribute, namely that they were judged to have it by following their fathers, so they were believers by judgment, owing to their youth and the faith of their fathers. A young child is judged to be a believer by following one of his parents who is a believer. But all of this, as you see, is far-fetched. It has also been said that the relative clause is conjoined to "hūr" (maidens of Paradise), and the meaning is: We paired them with the maidens and with those who believed, that is, with the companions and associates among them. Thus they enjoy at times the company of the maidens, and at other times the company of the believing brethren. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and We made them follow﴾ is a conjunction upon ("We married them"). His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿with faith﴾ is connected to what follows it, meaning: by means of a great faith of lofty station, which is the faith of the fathers, "We joined their offspring to their ranks," even though they do not deserve them, as a favour to them and to their fathers, so that their joy may be completed and their bliss perfected. Or it means: by means of a faith of lowly station, which is the faith of the offspring, as if it were said: with some measure of faith that does not qualify them for the rank of the fathers, We joined them to them.

The position of al-Zamakhsharī is clearly in favour of conjoining it to "hūr." He mentioned it as a first possibility, but Abū Ḥayyān criticised it, saying that no one would imagine this except this man, and that it is a non-Arab imagination, contrary to the understanding of pure Arabs such as Ibn ʿAbbās and others. It has been said in response that this is partisanship on his part. The fair view is that the obvious reading is that it is a resumption, and that the best and most suitable interpretation of the verse for the context is what has preceded.

Abū ʿAmr read "wa-atbaʿnāhum" with a hamza that is cut and a fatḥa, a sukūn on the *tāʾ*, a nūn after the *ʿayn* and an alif after it, meaning: We made them followers of them in faith. He also read "dhurriyyātahum" as a plural in the accusative. Ibn ʿĀmir read it the same way in the nominative. Someone read "dhirriyyātihim" with a kasra on the *dhāl*, and "wa-ittabaʿat-hum dhurriyyatuhum" with the *tāʾ* of the feminine subject, with "dhurriyyatahum" in the accusative as the object. Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Kathīr read "ālatnāhum" with a kasra on the *lām*, from *alita yaʾlatu*, like *ʿalima yaʿlamu*. According to the reading of the majority it is from the pattern of *ḍaraba yaḍribu*. Ibn Hurmuz read "ālatnāhum" from *ālata yu'litu*, with the *alif* of the verb form of "to wrong." Ibn Masʿūd and Ubayy read "li-tnāhum" from *lāta yalītu*, and this is the reading of Ṭalḥa and al-Aʿmash. It was also reported from Shibl and Ibn Kathīr, and from Ṭalḥa and al-Aʿmash as well, "lu-tnāhum," with a fatḥa on the *lām*. Sahl said: it is not permitted to put a fatḥa on the *lām* without an *alif* under any circumstances. He also rejected "ālatnāhum" with the *madd*, saying: it is not transmitted from anyone, nor does any exegesis or Arabic usage indicate it. This is not what he claimed. Rather, the lexicographers have transmitted *ālata* with the *madd*, as Hurmuz read. It was also read "wa-mā walatnāhum," from *walata yalitu*. The meaning of all of these is one. The verb *alita* also comes with the meaning of "to be harsh." It is reported that a man stood before ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, and admonished him, and he said: "Do not be harsh (*lā taʾlit*) toward the Commander of the Faithful," meaning: do not be harsh toward him.

﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned﴾, that is, for his earning and his deeds, ﴿in pledge﴾, that is, pledged with God. It is as if earning were like a debt, and the soul of the servant were like the pledge, and the pledge is not released until the debt is paid. If the deed is righteous, then the debt has been paid, because a righteous deed is accepted by its Lord, Glorified is He, and ascends to Him, Mighty and Majestic. If it is other than that, there is no payment, and so no release, since nothing but the good ascends to Him, Glorified is He. For this reason He, Majestic and Exalted, said: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned, except the people of the right﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:38–39]. The meaning is that every soul is held in pledge by its earning before God, Exalted is He, unreleased, except the people of the right, for they have freed their necks by what they made good of their earnings. The connection on this reading is that when He, Glorified is He, mentioned the condition of the righteous, and that He, Mighty and Majestic, had made ready for them the reward and the bounty, He followed this with this statement to indicate that they had freed their necks and delivered them, while others remained punished, because they did not free their necks. Its outward position would have been after His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He is the Good, the Merciful﴾ [al-Ṭūr 52:28], so that it would form a statement returning to the condition of the two groups, the summoned and the righteous. But it was placed as an interruption between the rewards of the righteous, following the mention of the abundant provision of what has been prepared for them. Al-Ṭībī said in *al-Kashf*: it is so that it indicates that deliverance is also from some of their rewards, and it follows that the absence of deliverance is the recompense of the opposing party by way of implication. Its placement is that of a parenthetical clause (*iʿtirāḍ*), to confirm the abundance of what was enumerated, since it only occurs after deliverance. In it is an implication that the joining of the children was by way of favour to the fathers, not to the children from the outset, because favour is a branch of deliverance, and these are the ones who were delivered and so deserved favour. To make it a clarifying resumption (*istiʾnāf bayānī*) for this meaning, as al-Ṭībī did, is far-fetched.

It has also been said that "held in pledge" (*rahīn*) is an adjective of the form *faʿīl* in the sense of the active participle, and the meaning is: every person is, by what he has earned, pledged (*rāhin*), that is, lasting and enduring. In *al-Irshād* it is said that this is more suitable to the context, since permanence requires that there be no separation between a person and his deed, and necessarily no reduction of the fathers' reward. So the sentence is an explanation of what precedes it. You know that *faʿīl* in the sense of *mafʿūl* (passive) comes more quickly to mind, so considering it is preferable, and its connection to the context is more fitting and more subtle, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verse 22–23:

﴿And We increased them in fruit and meat, of whatever they desire.﴾ That is: We added to them, over and above what they had of the beginnings of luxury, time after time, of the various kinds of blessings and the diverse sorts of bounties, of whatever they desire. The original sense of al-madd (extension, lengthening) is "pulling," and from it comes al-muddah (a period of time that extends); then it became common for increase. Al-imdad (supplying) became predominantly used for what is loved, and al-madd for what is disliked. And its being "time after time" is understood from the very meaning of al-madd itself. ﴿They pass around among themselves a cup﴾ That is: they pass it back and forth to one another in Paradise, they and their companions, passing it in playful pulling, as those drinking companions (al-nada'mi) do among themselves in this world, out of the intensity of their joy. Al-Akhtal said:

I contended with him over the purest wine, the wine of the morning, when the rooster had crowed and the time of the night-traveler's encounter had come.

It has been said: the contending (al-tanazu') is a metaphor for taking and handing. The word kas (cup) is feminine by transmitted usage, like khamr (wine). According to the well-known view, it is not called kas unless it is full of wine or nearly full. It may also be used for the wine itself metaphorically, by the relation of adjacency. Al-Raghib said: al-kas is the vessel together with what is in it of drink, and each of the two, when alone, is also called kas. Some interpreters explained it here as the vessel with the wine in it, and others as the wine itself. The first is more suitable to the passing back and forth; the second matches His saying, glorified is He: ﴿there is no idle talk therein﴾, that is, in its drinking, since they do not speak during drinking with idle talk and worthless speech. ﴿Nor any sinful word﴾, and they do not do what would make its doer sinful, that is, what would be attributed to sin had they done it in the abode of obligation, as is the habit of drinking companions in this world. Rather, they speak words of wisdom and fine speech, and they do what noble people do. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "lā laghwa" and "wa lā ta'thīma" with a fatha on both.

﴿And there will circulate among them﴾ — that is, with the cup — ﴿young boys belonging to them﴾ — that is, slaves specially attached to them, as the lām indicates. He did not say "their young boys" (ghilmānahum) with a possessive construction, lest it be imagined that they are those who used to serve them in this world, so that everyone who served someone in this world would fear that he would be his servant in Paradise, and would grieve that he remains a follower. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verses 25–26:

﴿And they approach one another, questioning each other.﴾ That is, each of them asks the other about his states and his deeds, so that each one is both questioner and questioned. It is not that a specific one of them asks a specific other. Then, this questioning takes place in Paradise, as is the apparent meaning. (And "in our family") it has been said: it may be a metaphor for this having been in the world; and it may be an explanation that their apprehension existed among them and among their families, because they followed them customarily, and it would be

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verses 27–28:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So Allah has been gracious to us﴾, i.e., with mercy and success, ﴿and has protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾, i.e., the punishment of the Fire, which penetrates the pores like the penetration of the samum, and the samum is the well-known hot wind. Although the aspect of resemblance is stronger in the Fire, the samum wind is better known to them since they witness it in this world, so it was made the object of comparison. Al-Hasan said: "al-Samum" is one of the names of Hell, general to them and to their people. So the meaning is an explanation of what Allah, may He be exalted, has bestowed upon them as grace, namely that their families followed them. It has also been said: ﴿among our families﴾ was mentioned to establish their fear at all times and circumstances by way of greater priority, for being among their families is ordinarily a place of security. I see no harm in this, yes, this would be so, because asking about what they were singled out for in honor rather than their families is not significant. It has also been said: perhaps the better option is to take this as an indication of compassion toward the creatures of Allah, may He be exalted, just as His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Indeed, we used to invoke Him before﴾ to the end, is an indication of the glorification of the command of Allah, may He be exalted. The conjunction was omitted by making the second clause an explanation of the first, claiming exaggeration regarding the necessity of the inseparability of each of them from the other, and what is in it is not hidden. What appears to me is that this is an indication of hope, and the omission of the conjunction is for the purpose of enumerating what they used to be upon, i.e., "Indeed, we used to worship Him, may He be exalted, before that and ask Him for protection." ﴿Indeed He is the Most Kind﴾, i.e., the one who does good, which is what his derivation from al-birr (kindness) with all its forms indicates, since they all return to goodness. Like "barra fi yaminihi," i.e., he was truthful, because truthfulness is goodness in itself and entails goodness to others. "Abarra Allahu hajjahu," i.e., He accepted it, because acceptance is goodness and increase. "Abarra fulan 'ala ashabihi," i.e., he rose above them, because it generally arises from goodness toward them. ﴿So remind﴾, that is, remain steadfast in the reminding you are already doing, with what has been revealed to you of the verses and the Wise Reminder, and do not be concerned with what they say of the falsehoods that contain no good.

﴿So you are not, by the grace of your Lord, a kahin (soothsayer)﴾. The kahin is one who reports the unseen by means of a kind of conjecture. Al-Raghib restricted the kahin to one who reports hidden past events in this manner, and the 'arraf (diviner) to one who reports future events in this manner. What is well known about kahanah (soothsaying) is seeking aid from the jinn in reporting the unseen. The ba' in ﴿bi-kahin﴾ is extra (*mazidah*) for emphasis, meaning: you are not a kahin. ﴿Nor a madman﴾. Scholars differed about the ba' in ﴿bi-ni'mati﴾. Abu al-Baqa said it is for accompaniment (*lil-mulabasah*), and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), its governing element being kahin or majnun. The meaning would be: you are not a kahin nor a madman, while being accompanied by your Lord's grace, and this is a constant circumstance, since the peace and blessings of God be upon him was always accompanied by the grace of his Lord, mighty and majestic. It was also said that the ba' is for oath, so that ﴿ni'matu rabbika﴾ is the thing sworn by, and the answer of the oath is what is understood from the sentence, namely: you are not a soothsayer nor a madman. This is like your saying: "Zayd is not standing, by God," which is far-fetched. In my view, the closer opinion is that the ba' is causal (*lil-sababiyyah*), and it is connected to the content of the sentence. The meaning is: soothsaying and madness have been negated from you because of God the Exalted's grace upon you. This is like your saying: "I am not poor, by God the Exalted's praise and His enriching of me." The intent is to refute the one who said this and to nullify their claim concerning him, peace and blessings of God be upon him. Otherwise, there is no favour upon him, may God bless him and grant him peace, in the negation of what was mentioned, given that its negation applies to most people. It was also said: the favour lies in the negation of that because of the grace, which is meant to be what he, may God bless him and grant him peace, was given of truthfulness in prophethood and soundness of intellect, which no one before him had been given. Those who say this are the disbelievers, may God curse them, how are they turned away! Among those who said "kahin" was Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, and among those who said "majnun" was 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt.

﴿Or do they say﴾, meaning: rather, do they say ﴿he is a poet﴾, meaning: he is a poet. ﴿We await for him﴾, meaning: we wait for him ﴿for the misfortunes of fate (rayb al-manun)﴾. Al-manun means fate (al-dahr). It is on the pattern fa'ul (فَعَوْلٌ) from al-mann, meaning "cutting off," because it cuts off lives and other things. From this comes the phrase habl manin (حَبَلٌ مَنِينٌ), meaning a severed rope. Rayb is a verbal noun from raabahu, meaning he troubled him. It is used here to mean the calamities and vicissitudes of fate, because they disturb souls, and it is expressed by the verbal noun for emphasis. It is also permissible that it comes from raba 'alayhi al-dahr, meaning fate befell him, and the intended meaning of its befalling is his destruction.

Interpreting al-manun as fate is narrated from Mujahid, and the verse of the poet supports it:

"Await for her the misfortunes of fate, perhaps she will be divorced one day, or her husband will die."

And the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Does he lament from fate and its misfortune? *** Yet fate does not blame the one who laments."

It is said: its apparent meaning is that, and so is the saying of al-A'sha:

"If he saw a man, al-A'sha, harmed by him, *** the misfortune of fate and a fate that is afflicted and deranged."

For this reason al-Jawhari cited it as evidence for it. Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn Abbas that it is interpreted as death. The word is shared between the two meanings. Al-Marzuqi said in his commentary on the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb mentioned above: al-manun may be meant as fate, in which case it is masculine, and the narration would be raybahu; it may be meant as death (al-maniyyah), in which case it is feminine, and it has been narrated as raybuha. It may also take a plural pronoun to intend the kinds of deaths, and its rayb is their descent. End of quotation, so do not be heedless of this. It is also from al-mann in the sense of cutting off, for death cuts off hopes and pleasures, and for this reason it is said: death cuts off hope. The misfortune of al-manun may mean the descent of death. It is also permissible that it means the occurrence of death, with the idafah (construct) being explanatory.

It is narrated that the Quraysh gathered in Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh), and their opinions about him ﷺ multiplied, until one of them said, and they were the Banu Abd al-Dar, as al-Dahhak said: "Await for him the misfortunes of fate, for he is a poet, and he will perish just as Zuhayr, al-Nabigha and al-A'sha perished." They dispersed upon this statement, and then the verse was revealed.

Zayd ibn Ali read yutarabbas (يُتَرَبَّصُ) with ya' and in the passive voice. It was also read as raybun (رَيْبٌ) in the nominative, as a substitute for the agent.

Say: "Wait." This is a mockery of them and a threat to them. "Indeed, I am with you among those who wait." I wait for your destruction just as you wait for my destruction. In this is a noble promise of their destruction. "Or do their intellects (aḥlāmuhum) command them?" That is, their reasons ('uqūl). The Quraysh used to claim to be the people of ḥilm (forbearance and sound judgment) and of intellect (nuhā). This is according to what al-Jāḥiẓ said, because the whole world comes to them and mixes with them, and by this intellect is made complete. It is completed by travel, by seeing different lands and varied places, and by keeping company with people of differing characters. Their aim was achieved without hardship. It was said to 'Amr ibn al-'Āṣ: "What is the matter with your people, that they did not believe, when God the Exalted has described them as possessing intellect?" He said: "Those are intellects which God, mighty and majestic, has outwitted (kādahā)." That is, tawfīq (divine success and guidance) did not accompany them, so they did not believe and disbelieved. "I do not see in the verse any indication of the superiority of their intellects," and perhaps it indicates the opposite of that.

"By this" refers to the contradiction in their speech. The soothsayer and the poet are people of complete intellect and keen acuity, whereas the madman has his intellect veiled and his thinking disordered. This indicates that these people, because of their bewilderment and partisanship, fell into ḥayṣ bayṣ (confusion and perplexity) until their intellects were disturbed and their statements contradicted one another, and they gave the lie to themselves without realizing it. The attribution of commanding to the intellects is a metaphor (majāz) for their leading to it, through the relation of causation, as has been said. It has also been said that the intellects were made to command by way of implicit metaphor (istiʿāra makniyya), in which intellects are likened to an obeyed ruler, an implicit comparison held in the soul, and the act of commanding is affirmed for them by way of imaginative representation (takhyīl).

"Or are they a people who transgress?" That is, they exceed the limits in obstinacy and stubborn opposition, and do not circle around right guidance and rectitude. Therefore they say what they say of falsehoods that are fortified and lie outside the sphere of reason. Mujahid read: "Rather, they (bal hum)."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verse 33:

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ That is, he fabricated it (ikhtalaqahu) from his own self (min tilqa'i nafsihi).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is that he attributed to another the claim that he (the Prophet) had said it; so it is an expression for a specific kind of lie, and the object pronoun refers to the Qur'an. ﴿Rather, they do not believe.﴾ Because of their disbelief and obstinacy, they throw out these falsehoods. How could it be otherwise, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was none other than one man from among the Arabs? So how could he bring what all the nations, both Arab and non-Arab, were unable to produce?

﴿So let them produce a statement like it﴾, resembling the Qur'an in the qualities that it alone possesses, in both its composition (*nazm*) and its meaning, ﴿if they are truthful﴾ in what they claim. Their truthfulness in that would require their capacity to produce its like, since they share with him (peace be upon him) humanity and the Arabic language, and since they have long practiced sermons and poetry, been constantly engaged in the methods of verse and prose, and taken great care to memorize events and days. There is no doubt that capacity for something necessitates producing it and motivates the command to do so. Thus the statement is a rebuttal of the claims made about him (peace be upon him). The Qur'an issues the challenge (*tahaddi*), so when they are challenged and fail, it is known that what they said is refuted and that the claim (*al-mudda'a*) is sound. It is also permitted that the verse is a rebuttal of their claim that he merely fabricated (*taqawwul*) in particular, since other claims mentioned earlier, including soothsaying (*kihana*), are clearly more corrupt, as is evident. Moreover, when the corruption of the claim of fabrication becomes evident, the corruption of the others becomes evident by implication.

Al-Jahdari and Abu al-Sammal read ﴿بِحَدِيثٍ مِثْلِهِ﴾ with the *idafa* (genitive construction) as *bi-hadithin mithlihi*, meaning: "with a statement of a man like the Messenger (ﷺ)" in that he was unlettered, had not accompanied the people of knowledge, and had not traveled from his land; or "his like" in that he is one of them, so there is no impossibility that there might be among the Arabs someone like him in eloquence. Let him then produce what he produced; but they will never be able to do so, ever.

﴿Or were they created from nothing?﴾ That is: or did they come into being and determine this wondrous determination without any determiner and creator? Al-Tabari said: the meaning is, "Or were they created from something non-living, so that they are not commanded or forbidden, like inanimate objects." And it was said: the meaning is, "Or were they created without a cause (ʿillah) and without a purpose (ghayah) of reward and punishment, so for that reason they do not hear." The "min" (from) in it indicates causation, and according to what preceded it, it indicates the starting point (ibtidaʾ al-ghayah). The view relied upon among the opinions is what we have mentioned earlier, and God willing, further clarification of it will come later. It is supported by His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Or are they the creators?﴾ That is, those who created themselves, and for that reason they do not worship God, Mighty and Majestic, nor do they heed His Messenger, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, since on both views the fitting correspondence does not become apparent. And that the intended meaning is "they created themselves" is indicated by the words of God, exalted is He:

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verse 36:

﴿Or were the heavens and the earth created by them?﴾ [al-Tur: 36] For if the generality were intended, given the omission of the object, the fine balance of the contrast would not appear either. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The meaning is: are they the ones who created things, and so they are arrogant on account of that? Then he singled out the heavens and the earth from those things, for their greatness and nobility among created beings. In this there is what you have heard." ﴿Rather, they are not certain.﴾ That is, when they are asked, "Who created you and created the heavens

and the earth?" they say, "God," but they are not certain of what they say. For if they were certain, they would not turn away from worshipping Him, the Exalted, since whoever knows his Creator and is certain of Him obeys and submits to Him.

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 52, verse 37:

﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord?﴾ That is, the treasuries of His provision and His mercy, exalted is He, so that they could bestow prophethood on whomever they wish and withhold it from whomever they wish. Al-Rummani said: "His treasuries, exalted is He, are His capabilities, glorified is He." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The meaning is: Or do they have independence from Allah, exalted is He, in all matters? For wealth, health, honour and other such things are among the treasuries of Allah, exalted is He." Al-Zuhri said: "By the treasuries he means knowledge," and Abu Hayyan approved of this view. What is known of his position will come later, if Allah wills.

﴿Or are they the controllers?﴾ That is, the lords who prevail, so that they could manage the affair of lordship (rububiyyah, the divine sovereignty over creation) and build affairs upon their own will and desire. The *musaytir* is the one who prevails and dominates. Ibn 'Abbas's statement has this meaning: "The one who dominates, the overpowering." *Sayṭara 'ala kadha* means that he watched over it and took charge of it. The word is not a diminutive, as some suppose. Only five words follow this pattern (*fu'ayil*, with the doubled-letter form): four are adjectives, namely *muhaymin*, *musaytir*, *mubayqir* and *mubaytir*, and one is a noun, *mujaymir*, which is the name of a mountain.

Most readers recited *al-Musaytirun* with the *sad* (ﺹ), because of the presence of the emphatic letter (*harf al-isti'la*, a letter pronounced with the tongue raised toward the palate), which is the *ta'* (ﻁ). Khalaf, transmitting from Hamza, and Khallad, transmitting from him, recited the *sad* with *ishmam* (a slight rounding of the lips toward the *damma*), in contrast to the *zay* (ﺯ) reading.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verse 38–39:

﴿Or do they have a ladder﴾ It is that by which one reaches high places, so that safety is hoped for through it; then the term was made a name for everything by which one reaches a lofty thing, such as a cause (sabab). That is: Or do they have a ladder set up to the heaven? ﴿by which they listen﴾ That is, ascending on it. This is on the basis that the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa'l-majrur) is connected to a specific omitted verb-like complement (kawn khass mahdhuf) that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the locative sense (al-zarfiyyah) is in its literal sense. It has also been said that it is connected to "yastami'un" (they listen), on the basis of its being construed with the meaning of ascending (al-su'ud).

Abu Hayyan said: That is, they listen upon it or from it, since prepositions may stand in for one another. The object of "yastami'un" is omitted, that is, the speech of God Most High. It has been said: If it were treated as intransitive, it would be permissible. ﴿So let their listener bring a clear authority﴾ That is, a manifest proof that verifies his listening. ﴿Or does He have daughters while you have sons?﴾ This is a rebuke to them and a belittling of their intellects. It also signifies that whoever holds this opinion scarcely counts among the intelligent, let alone ascends to the realm of the dominion (malakut) and hears the speech of the Possessor of Might and Majesty. The shift to the second person in address is to intensify the denunciation and reproach.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verses 40–41:

﴿Or do you ask them for a payment?﴾ That is, for conveying the message. This is a return to addressing the Prophet (ﷺ) and a turning away from them. ﴿So they are﴾ because of that ﴿burdened with debt﴾: "maghram" is a mimi verbal noun from "ghurm" and "gharama" (indebtedness, liability), which, as al-Raghib said, is the harm that befalls a person's wealth without any wrongdoing on his part. So the phrase is constructed with an omitted noun, meaning "from the obligation of a debt." Al-Zamakhshari explained it as a person taking on what is not incumbent upon him, so no omission is needed. However, what the language requires is the first view. ﴿Burdened﴾ means they are made to bear the weight, and therefore they do not follow you.

﴿Or do they have the unseen, so that they write it down?﴾ That is, the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), in which the unseen matters are recorded, so that they copy from it and inform people of it. This was said by Ibn Abbas. Ibn Atiyyah said: "Or do they have knowledge of the unseen, so that they establish for the people, as law, what they claim?" This refers to the worship of idols, the releasing of the sawa'ib (free-roaming animals), and other such practices of their conduct. Qatadah said: "﴿Or do they have the unseen﴾ so that they know when Muhammad (ﷺ), whom they are waiting for, will die?" Some of the scholars interpreted "yaktubun" (they write) as "yahkumun" (they judge).

Some of the scholars interpreted "yaktubun" (they write) as "yahkumun" (they judge).

[p. 39]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verse 42:

﴿Or do they intend a plot?﴾ against you and against your law (shar'). This refers to what they did against him (ﷺ) at the Dar al-Nadwa (the council house of the Quraysh), which is well known from the biographies (al-sirah). This is among the foretellings of the unseen (al-ikhbar bil-ghayb), for the affair of the Dar al-Nadwa took place at the time of the Hijrah (emigration), while the revelation of this surah came before it, as the reports indicate. ﴿Then those who disbelieved﴾ are those already mentioned, who intended to plot against him, peace and blessings be upon him.

The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) was placed in the position of their pronoun in order to record (al-tasjil) against them the disbelief contained in the relative clause (al-silah), and to show the disbelief as the reason for the ruling. It is also permissible that the reference be to all the disbelievers, with these people included in it in the first place. ﴿They are the ones who will be ensnared﴾, meaning those upon whom their plot recoils and whose harm returns to them, not those whom they intended to plot against. For those people, the harm was their being killed on the day of Badr in the fifteenth year of prophethood. It is said that for this reason the word (أمْ) occurs repeated here fifteen times, to indicate what has been mentioned. Something similar to this, according to al-Shihab, is not to be deemed remote among the Qur'anic miracles, even though the connection to such a thing is hidden and its relevance is even more hidden. It is also permissible that the meaning be: they are the ones defeated in the plot, [namely] whoever I plotted against, so I outplotted them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verses 43–44:

﴿Or do they have a god other than Allah?﴾ (who would) help them and protect them from His punishment, the Exalted, the Majestic.

﴿Glory be to Allah above what they associate with Him.﴾ That is, (exalted) above their association (of partners with Him), on the reading that ما (mā) is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah) particle; or (exalted) above the partnership of that which they associate, on the reading that it is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), with an understood genitive noun (muḍāf muqaddar) before it and an omitted returning pronoun (ʿāʾid maḥdhūf).

﴿And if they should see a fragment (kisfan)﴾ — a piece. It is singular, and it has been read throughout the Qur'an as kisfan and kisafan, both as a plural and as a singular, except here, where it is read only in the singular. Its tanwin is for emphasis (tafkhīm), meaning: "And if they should see a great fragment"

﴿falling from the sky﴾ — to punish them.

﴿they would say﴾ — out of the extremity of their rebellion and obstinacy:

﴿"It is (merely) a cloud piled up."﴾ — that is, it is a cloud (saḥāb) (that is) ﴿marköm﴾, piled up, layered, one part upon another. That is, they are so deep in rebellion that even if We were to drop upon them, as they demanded, or if the sky were to fall upon us in pieces, as they claimed, they would say, "It is a layered cloud that is raining on us," and they would not believe that it was a fragment falling as a punishment upon them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 52, verses 43–44:

﴿Or do they have a god other than Allah?﴾ (who would) help them and protect them from His punishment, the Exalted, the Majestic.

﴿Glory be to Allah above what they associate with Him.﴾ That is, (exalted) above their association (of partners with Him), on the reading that ما (mā) is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah) particle; or (exalted) above the partnership of that which they associate, on the reading that it is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), with an understood genitive noun (muḍāf muqaddar) before it and an omitted returning pronoun (ʿāʾid maḥdhūf).

﴿they would say﴾ — out of the extremity of their rebellion and obstinacy:
